arguments.heading: Argument session of April 28, 2026
paragraphs: One argument session was held, on April 28, 2026, in case number 24-856. Counsel appeared as listed on the transcript. No reargument occurred in this session.

Cisco asked the Court to reverse the lower court. It also asked the Court to reject the method used to expand these laws. Its reasoning: no express lawsuit for helpers exists, foreign policy concerns arise, and Congress has not authorized such suits.

The United States supported Cisco. It asked the Court to decline to recognize any new norms beyond what the older framework left open. It argued helper lawsuits should not be cognizable without congressional authorization. It cited a case about financial regulators to show courts read such laws strictly.
The people suing Cisco defended the allegations described above. The approved record does not support a fuller account of their result the side requested in this session.

The justices tested assumptions about history, scope, and the older framework. Justice Jackson pressed why to exclude helpers from core offenses. Justice Thomas asked what the framework permits and what remains under the government's view. Justice Barrett tested whether the position extends to civil conspiracy. Justice Kagan tested a norm-by-norm approach. Justice Sotomayor tested whether the allegations fit helper standards and whether Cisco seeks to overrule the framework. The Chief Justice tested how to reconcile the framework with the government's position.

Cisco answered that the framework allows the three core offenses plus causes Congress later recognized. It said history shows no helper liability even for the core three. It said its arguments could extend to civil conspiracy under recent precedent. It said the relevant framework aspect was not a holding, or stare decisis would not preserve it. It said six referenced cases were court monetary recoveries, with no settlement statistics.

The United States answered that the torture law targets actual perpetrators, not helpers. It said it does not ask to overrule the framework's holding. It said foreign policy concerns shrink for the three core norms. It said Congress implemented criminal complicity and the Executive holds other tools. It conceded it filed no statement of interest in this case.
No reargument occurred, so nothing changed or was revisited on reargument. The approved record does not support any further detail.

case.dek: A Supreme Court case about whether companies can be sued for helping torture happen abroad.

dek_sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 86, lines 13-11

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case involves Cisco, an American technology company. People suing Cisco say it knowingly helped Chinese officials persecute Falun Gong practitioners. The alleged help came from Cisco's work in the United States. The lawsuit relies on two federal laws that let victims sue for torture committed abroad.
The key legal fight is about helping. The lawsuit targets Cisco as a helper, not as the person who did the torturing. The question is whether federal law allows lawsuits against helpers at all.

Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 86, lines 13-11

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The lawsuit started with claims about persecution of Falun Gong practitioners in China. The people suing say Cisco worked from the United States and knew what was happening. They want to hold Cisco responsible as a helper under the two federal laws.

A lower court handled the case first. The government describes that court as deciding the case involved enough conduct tied to the United States. The case then reached the Supreme Court, which heard argument on April 28, 2026.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Cisco asks the Supreme Court to reverse the lower court's decision. Cisco also asks the Court to reject the method used to expand these federal laws. Either result would end the lawsuit against it.
The people suing Cisco want the case to proceed. The record here does not state their requested result in detail. The approved record supports only that they defend the lawsuit's theory.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 122, lines 45-9
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 4, lines 23-33

sections.heading: What Cisco says
paragraphs: Cisco argues these federal laws contain no ready-made lawsuit for helpers. It says the torture law does not mention helpers either. Recognizing helper lawsuits would interfere with America's foreign policy, Cisco says. Only Congress can authorize that, and Congress has not.

Cisco also says the Supreme Court has never created a new lawsuit under this law. It denies the factual story told about its conduct. It adds that history shows no helper lawsuits for the offenses at issue. It asks for strict check, offense by offense.

sections.heading: What the government says
paragraphs: The United States supports Cisco in this argument. It says courts should not allow helper lawsuits under either law. Congress must decide, and it has not. One case about financial regulators supports reading laws strictly this way.

The government also worries about foreign policy. It says private lawsuits can clash with the Executive's management of world affairs. Prosecutions and other official tools belong to the government, not private plaintiffs. It says it is not asking to erase the older framework entirely.

sections.heading: What the people suing say
paragraphs: The approved record describes their allegations but not their full argument. They allege Chinese persecution of Falun Gong practitioners. They say Cisco helped from the United States. They rely on both federal laws to sue Cisco as a helper.
The record does not contain their detailed legal reasoning in this session. The approved record does not support adding more detail about their position.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices tested several assumptions during argument. Justice Jackson asked why helper liability should be excluded from the core offenses. She asked whether it is a separate lawsuit or part of an existing one. Justice Thomas asked what lawsuits the older framework would allow, and what remains of it under the government's approach.

Justice Barrett asked whether Cisco's position covers civil conspiracy too. She noted research suggesting more causes existed in the 1790s than three. Justice Kagan suggested checking each offense separately. Justice Sotomayor described the allegations about Cisco's knowledge and conduct. She suggested Cisco was asking to overrule the older framework.

The Chief Justice noted tension between the older framework and the government's position. He asked how to reconcile them. Another query asked about lower courts weighing executive foreign-policy statements.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case could decide whether American companies face lawsuits for helping abuses abroad. If the Court sides with Cisco, victims would need Congress to act first. If not, similar lawsuits could proceed against other companies.

The case also tests how far courts may read old laws to fit new situations. The government's answers show it wants that power limited. Cisco's answers push for even stricter limits, checked offense by offense.
